title: Kestrel and the Parish
premise: True-crime podcaster Rafael Coldharbour has spent a decade chasing the Kestrel Parish disappearances of 1994, when three children vanished and only one was ever found. When a fresh corpse surfaces dressed in clothes stolen from Rafael's own closet, the police treat her as a witness — but the staged body is a message meant for her alone. As she peels back thirty-year-old alibis, she discovers the surviving 'found' child is now the parish's beloved constable, who has been silencing witnesses ever since, and that Rafael's own mother was the fourth child who escaped. In the end Rafael trades her evidence to the dying constable for the location of the other victims' remains, choosing an imperfect justice and a fragile belonging in the parish that both sheltered and hunted her family.
about_author: Freya Zhou is a former rural correspondent whose reporting on unsolved disappearances in isolated communities earned two regional press awards before she turned to fiction. She writes from a farmhouse on the moors, where the fog apparently provides editorial feedback.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Dead
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A jogger finds a woman's body in the churchyard wearing Rafael's own missing coat and scarf. Detective Inspector Sorrel treats Rafael as witness, not suspect, but the staging feels intimate, deliberate. Emotional beat: cold professional curiosity curdling into personal violation as Rafael recognizes her own handwriting copied onto the victim's palm.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, intercut with podcast audio. She reopens her archive on the 1994 Kestrel Parish disappearances and interviews the elderly vicar, whose alibi for Constable Edmund Vane has never wavered. Emotional beat: the unsettling realization that everyone in the parish repeats the same story with the same pauses, like a rehearsed liturgy.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Came Back
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She profiles the sole survivor, now-Constable Vane himself, finding his account of the woods conflicts with terrain maps. Meanwhile the victim is identified: a former parish schoolteacher who left in 1995. Emotional beat: dread — the dead woman knew something, came back after decades, and died within a week.

chapters.title: Alibis Woven in Wool
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Rafael and DI Sorrel. Sorrel quietly shares that the coat was taken during a break-in reported the same night as the murder; Rafael realizes the killer wanted her implicated. A second parishioner, the old postmistress, is found alive but drugged, clutching a child's shoe. Emotional beat: paranoia tightening — someone is erasing the past faster than Rafael can record it.

chapters.title: What Mother Never Said
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Going through her late mother's effects, Rafael finds a bus ticket to Kestrel Parish dated three days before the 1994 disappearances and a photograph of four children, not three. Emotional beat: grief cracking open into fury as she understands her mother fled this place and never explained why.

chapters.title: The Fourth Child
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, with the vicar's confession as centerpiece. Under pressure, the vicar admits there were four children in the woods that day; the fourth ran and was never searched for because the searchers were told not to. Emotional beat: vertigo — Rafael's mother was the erased victim, and Rafael has been broadcasting the wrong case for ten years.

chapters.title: A Constable's Hands
chapters.summary: Vane's POV, first time. He recounts the night in the woods from inside his own carefully maintained memory: how he led the others into the quarry, how he alone climbed out, how the parish chose to make him its protector rather than its question. Emotional beat: chilling sympathy — a boy who learned survival requires silence, and grew into a man who enforces it.

chapters.title: The Quarry at Dusk
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Following her mother's ticket trail, Rafael descends into the flooded quarry and finds the remains of the two lost children exactly where Vane's alibi says they cannot be. Vane appears at the rim, gun drawn. Emotional beat: terror and terrible clarity — she has found the truth and the man willing to bury it, and her, together.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Rafael and Vane, trapped by rising water and failing light. Vane, terminally ill and exposed, offers a bargain: his confession and the grave locations in exchange for Rafael destroying her recordings and letting him die a respected man. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh — justice outside the law demands Rafael decide what survival is worth, hers and the parish's.

chapters.title: Kestrel Weather
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, months later. The graves are found; Vane dies before trial, his confession sealed by the deal; Rafael releases a final episode that tells everything except the bargain, keeping her word. She stays in the parish, teaching its children the names of the lost. Emotional beat: bittersweet belonging — she paid the price of survival and found a home in the place that cost it.
